ABSTRACT
High-performance computing demands efficient and scalable interconnections. Although crossbar networks offer high parallel
bandwidth, their 𝑂(𝑛2) costs are prohibitively expensive. Multi-stage networks provide scalability with 𝑂(𝑛log 𝑛) cost, yet they may
block certain routing patterns. Rearrangeable multistage networks (RMNs) have emerged as a cost-effective solution, enabling
internal connection rearrangements to make all paths accessible without network blocking. However, discovering optimal rear-
rangement strategies remains a challenge for unblocking large-scale (256 connections) reconfigurable networks. We advance the
state of the art by effectively managing workloads with over 50% without blocking. When nearly all connections are required, we
introduce routing strategies to rearrange existing connections. In the presence of multicast, where the configuration space exceeds
10671, we propose novel strategies employing simulated annealing for placement and Monte Carlo tree search for routing to pri-
oritize multicast connections, which simultaneously maximize the number of connections by minimizing conflicts and reducing
the number of extra stages. To the best of our knowledge, we first demonstrate that the Benes network is not rearrangeable under
multicast conditions. We propose exploring the rearrangeability of shuffle exchanges with additional network stages.

employs a butterfly multi-stage topology. Furthermore, graph
reconfigurable hardware exemplifies the potential of multi-stage
interconnects. A single-source shortest path accelerator [6] uti-

when processing vertex data in FPGA HBMs, securing the
14th position in the Graph 500 benchmark for data-intensive
applications—the highest ranking for a single FPGA. Sparse
matrix-vector multiplication (SpMV) on FPGAs has emerged
as a critical research area due to its extensive applications in
Artificial Intelligence (AI). A multi-stage approach [7] effectively
replaces the crossbar, mitigating interconnection bottlenecks
and substantially improving overall performance.
Beyond interconnecting FPGA accelerator HBM channels,
multi-stage networks can also enhance the performance of
spatial computing by connecting processing elements. The
Regraph accelerator [8] employs a multi-stage approach to con-
nect processing elements for solving graph algorithm problems,
including PageRank, Breadth-First Search (BFS), and Closeness
Centrality. Silva et al. [9] proposed a framework to support
polynomial runtime mapping of dataflow spatial applications
in CPU-FPGA platforms. These previous works motivate the
study of multi-stage limits and scalability. Although multi-stage
network studies originated in the 1950s–1960s and were a hot
research topic in the 1990s, their analytical exploration has been
limited. The complexity of creating analytical models and the
huge search space—exceeding 10671 possible configurations for
256 connections—have significantly hindered comprehensive
analysis. Consequently, few in-depth studies [10–13] have been
presented despite the architectural potential.
The first contribution of this work is to identify research gaps,
characterize them, and propose solutions. Multi-stage Intercon-
nection Networks (MINs) could operate in both circuit-switched
and packet-switched modes. Packet-based MINs require buffers,
and the bandwidth is limited to 50% [3, 4]. Can we reduce the
cost by operating in circuit-switched mode while maintaining
an unblocking network for traffic patterns beyond 50%? What
routing challenges persist in multi-stage networks? While Benes
networks are rearrangeable and could be unblocking with a lin-
ear routing algorithm [14], does this property hold for multicast
patterns? These research questions drive our investigation.
This work extends previous research [15] on multistage for spa-
tial parallel computing, which interconnects processing elements
through flexible architectures [9] capable of dynamic runtime
reconfiguration. Unlike the prior work that explored only greedy
approaches, we address several critical research gaps through
comprehensive investigation.
Our contributions are threefold. First, we formalize the place-
ment and routing of a parallel computation graph as a substring
matching problem. Second, we comprehensively profile the
placement and routing (P&R) process, identifying routing as the
primary computational bottleneck, where graph structures have
non-tree characteristics [16] with multicast patterns. Rearrange-
able networks like Benes networks can theoretically establish
connections between inputs and outputs, multicast patterns
dramatically increase routing complexity. Routing becomes an
NP-complete problem for Clos networks [17]. To address these
challenges, we propose novel routing strategies designed to
mitigate conflicts and reduce execution time through strategic
connection rearrangements.
Third, our research demonstrates the efficacy of Monte Carlo
and multicast ordering techniques, particularly in high-workload
routing scenarios exceeding 50% network capacity. Critically, and
to the best of our knowledge, we are the first to conclusively show
that the Benes network [14, 18] becomes blocking when con-
fronted with multicast routing patterns.
The structure of this paper is as follows: Section 2 describes the
CGRA mapping using a multi-stage approach and introduces the
mapping as a substring matching problem. Section 3 outlines the
placement strategies from previous work [15] based on a sim-
ple greedy routing approach. Additionally, we demonstrate that
Benes is blocking, and shuffle-exchange with log(𝑛) extra stages
could be rearrangeable in the presence of multicast. In Section 4,
novel routing strategies are presented, including Monte Carlo
Tree Search (MCTS). Section 5 details the main results. Finally,
Sections 6 and 7 discuss related work and conclude, respectively.

Background
2.1

Rearrangeable Multi-Stage
Interconnections
A multi-stage interconnection network (MIN) consists of stages
of programmable switches interconnected by a pattern. A MIN is
non-blocking in the strict sense if any input-output pair is always
connectable and does not depend on other connection pairs. A
MIN is broadly non-blocking if it follows a specific ordering rule
that permits adding a new connection without causing blocking
conflicts. A MIN is rearrangeable and non-blocking if rearranging
existing connections is required to accommodate new connec-
tions. Conversely, a MIN is blocking if it cannot establish con-
nections for all input-output pairs [19].

The Clos network, proposed in 1953 [20], can be either
non-blocking or rearrangeable, depending on the complexity of
its internal switches. A decade later, the Benes network [18] was
introduced, reducing switch complexity to 2 × 2 inputs/outputs.
Benes is a rearrangeable network with a polynomial rout-
ing algorithm [14]. However, its routability is limited in the
presence of multicast connections. Another decade later, the
shuffle-exchange or Omega network [21] emerged, designed to
be non-blocking for specific patterns. Omega features a simple
design with a regular interstage pattern and a straightforward
routing algorithm. Nonetheless, it becomes a blocking network
if there are log 𝑛stages, although it can be made rearrangeable
by adding log 𝑛extra stages, even in the presence of multicast.
However, the solution space becomes exponentially large even
for small values of 𝑛. For example, with 𝑛= 32, there are over
1035 configurations, and with 𝑛= 256, there are more than 10671
configurations.

Routing in Shuffle-Exchange Networks
This study analyzes the shuffle-exchange or Omega network due
to its regular pattern and straightforward connection routing
algorithm [21]. This network is a bit permutation network (BPN),
and it’s important to highlight that all BPNs, including the but-
terfly and bayan networks [22, 23], are considered equivalent.
Figure 1 shows an 𝑛= 8 or 8 × 8 shuffle-exchange network. An
𝑛× 𝑛network has log(𝑛) stages, each containing 𝑛
2 2 × 2 switching
elements. Therefore, for 𝑛= 8, there are 3 stages with 4 switch-
ing elements each, totaling 12 switches, which can achieve 212 =
4, 096 configurations. However, for 𝑛= 8, there are 8! = 40,320
possible one-to-one mappings from input to output. Thus, a log 𝑛
network is blocking because it cannot achieve all 40,320 permu-
tations with only 4,096 configurations.
Figure 1a illustrates the routing path from input 2 to output 6
in an 8 × 8 network. Initially, we concatenate the binary codes
of the input and output connections to form a routing word,
as depicted in Figure 1b, resulting in 010 110 . The routing
algorithm then slides a log(𝑛) = log(8) = 3-bit window across the
routing word, with each window generating an interstage line.
In our example, the path traverses line 5 = 101binary after the first
stage and line 3 = 011binary after the second stage to reach output
6 = 110binary. Therefore, the slicing windows in the routing word
are 0 101 10,01 011 0, and 010 110 .
Figure 1c depicts the network configuration after adding a new
connection from input 3 to output 4. The routing algorithm
must consider both the previous and new connections during
the traversal of the sliding window. All codes should be distinct
within the routing windows to avoid routing conflicts. In our
example, the connection pair 3 →4 utilizes lines 7 and 6 between
the stages, without conflict with lines 5 and 3 used by the connec-
tion pair 2 →6, as depicted in Figure 1c.
However, when adding another connection pair 1 →5, a conflict
arises in line 6 between stages 2 and 3, as depicted in Figure 1d,
highlighted in grey within the sliding window word. As men-
tioned, a 3-stage 8 × 8 network is blocked due to insufficient
switches to accommodate all permutations. Adding an extra stage
increases the number of switches from 12 to 16, and the possi-
ble configurations rise to 216 = 65, 536, surpassing the number
of permutations, which is 8! = 40, 320. However, even with this
augmentation, an 8 × 8 network remains insufficient to achieve
non-blocking or rearrangeable status [23].
Adding an extra stage introduces an additional bit in the rout-
ing word, which can be configured as 0 or 1 to prevent conflicts.
Figure 2a illustrates how to manage the three connections from

2.3
|
Multi-Stage Interconnections and CGRA
In this work, we examine the effectiveness of multi-stage
interconnection for mapping dataflow graphs onto parallel
architectures featuring 𝑛Processing Elements (𝑃𝐸𝑠). In parallel
computing, a processing element (PE) can range from a simple
logic gate or a basic compute unit, such as an adder, to a func-
tional unit like an ALU, or even a programmable computing unit
with an ALU, a local register bank, and configuration memory.
In some cases, it may encompass a complete processor. In this
work, the processing element refers to a functional unit, such
as an ALU, designed to perform binary operations. Addition-
ally, it is possible to integrate local configuration memory, a
feature commonly found in CGRA architectures. This mem-
ory supports techniques like modulo scheduling, enabling the
mapping of graphs larger than the number of PEs by allowing
time-multiplexed execution. The set of processing elements (PEs)
can be either homogeneous or heterogeneous, offering a signif-
icant advantage of multi-stage interconnection networks (MIN)
over grid-based architectures. Unlike grid-based designs, MIN
allows any PE to connect directly to any other PE, regardless of
their position. Each PE can independently execute instructions
and perform operations on data. The effectiveness of dataflow
graph mapping is determined by how well these PEs can handle
the assigned computational tasks and communicate with each
other through the interconnection network.
While mesh-based architectures help mitigate interconnection
costs to 𝑂(𝑐), the mapping process is NP-complete [24]. Exact
solutions utilizing integer linear programming or SAT solvers
exhibit scalability issues for graphs containing more than 30
nodes [25]. Despite recent advancements in mapping tech-
niques leveraging reinforcement learning and graph attention
networks [26], the mapping process still demands approximately
10 s and is constrained to graphs with fewer than 68 nodes. Fur-
thermore, these architectures have not yet been validated on real
devices. We select as a baseline architecture a coarse-grained
reconfigurable architecture (CGRA) proposed in reference [9],
comprising 128 𝑃𝐸𝑠, which have been successfully validated on
an FPGA using multi-stage networks. Hence, we propose evalu-
ating scenarios involving more than 100 nodes.
For ease of explanation, let’s consider a basic architecture with
four Processing Elements (𝑃𝐸𝑠). Each 𝑃𝐸has two inputs and
two outputs. The 𝑃𝐸𝑠are connected by an 8 × 8 multi-stage
network, depicted in Figure 3a. The mapping task is to allocate
each dataflow node onto a 𝑃𝐸(placement) and establish con-
nections using the multi-stage network (routing), as illustrated
in Figure 3b. In this mapping, nodes 𝐴, 𝐵, 𝐶, and 𝐷are assigned
to 𝑃𝐸𝑠0, 1, 2, and 3, respectively. The inputs/outputs of 𝑃𝐸𝑖are
linked to the network at positions 2 ⋅𝑖and 2 ⋅𝑖+ 1. It’s important
to note that a 𝑃𝐸output is an interconnect input, and vice
versa. This mapping requires the routing 0 →2, 0 →4, 2 →5,
and 3 →6 for the edges 𝐴→𝐵, 𝐴→𝐶, 𝐵→𝐶, and 𝐶→𝐷,
respectively, as depicted in Figure 3b. Given a particular place-
ment, generating a feasible routing can be challenging due
to network conflicts. Figure 3c showcases a novel placement
achieved by swapping nodes 𝐵and 𝐶, resulting in new routing
patterns. While this is a simplistic example, various design factors
need consideration, including the number of interconnection
stages, the types and quantities of 𝑃𝐸𝑠, and the input/output
permutation assignments.
The dataflow depicted in Figure 3 could, for example, imple-
ment a 1D stream vector convolution computation, where 𝐶𝑖=
3 × 𝐴𝑖+ 2 × 𝐴𝑖−1 and 𝐷𝑖= 4 × 𝐴2
𝑖−1, derived from a data stream
applied to node 𝐴. Examples of machine learning applications,
such as K-means clustering, convolution, and matrix multiplica-

Placement Strategies
It is well-known that placement decisions impact routing quality,
among other critical aspects [28]. In mesh-based Coarse-Grained
CGRA architectures, placing graphs with more than 40 nodes is
a challenging problem [29]. Existing multi-stage approaches [9]
can scale to 100 nodes, but they typically rely on greedy strate-
gies. We propose novel approaches: First profiling the inter-
connection to extract intrinsic properties and then designing
enhanced placement strategies. The proposed approaches can
handle heavy workloads by finding exact solutions while simul-
taneously reducing costs through minimal or no additional inter-
connection stages.
One approach to mitigate routing conflicts is to enhance the
placement strategy. Initially, it is important to understand the
network behavior better. Section 3.1 illustrates that specific
patterns present more significant routing challenges than others.
However, the vast solution space makes it challenging to create
analytical models for larger multi-stage networks [11]. There-
fore, we propose random sampling of patterns to measure routing
capabilities, as detailed in Section 3.2. Given the difficulty in
routing some patterns, placement strategies could evaluate code
assignment methods, as outlined in Section 3.3. Section 3.4 intro-
duces optimization algorithms based on heuristics to enhance
placement given the larger search space.

Blocking or Rearrangeable: Benes
and Shuffle-Exchange Networks
Benes [18] is a recursive network, as illustrated in Figure 6a,
for an 8 × 8 network that contains two 4 × 4 Benes subnetworks.
Each switch in the first stage connects to the upper and lower sub-
network. The last stage has the same property. This configuration
ensures that the Benes network is rearrangeable, and a polyno-
mial algorithm exists for this purpose [14]. However, to the best
of the authors’ knowledge, whether a Benes network is rearrange-
able in the presence of multicast remains an open question. The
Benes network is a simplification of the Clos network [20], which
is rearrangeable for multicast, though routing in such a network
is NP-complete [17].
We propose conducting an exhaustive search on 4 × 4 and 8 × 8
Benes and Shuffle-exchange networks in the presence of multi-
cast. Table 1 illustrates the routing capability of 4 × 4 and 8 × 8
networks with minimal size and one, two, or three additional lev-
els for the shuffle-exchange network. Given the recursive nature
of the Benes network, the only possible configuration for an 8 × 8
Benes network is with 5 stages, which has the exact cost of a
shuffle-exchange network with two extra levels.

out of 256 patterns, representing 43% of all patterns. Conversely,
a minimal 8 × 8 shuffle network encounters blocking for nearly

We evaluate four placement strategies for mapping graph nodes
to Processing Elements (𝑃𝐸𝑠). Let’s consider nodes 𝐴and 𝐵,
where there is a directed edge from 𝐴to 𝐵, and we assume
a sequential input/output code. The first strategy is just ran-
dom placement and routing. While a random approach may
appear less favorable than an ordered approach, such as sequen-
tial assignment, it performs better. The reason for this behavior
is that randomness helps prevent conflicts, given that input suf-
fixes and output prefixes do not exhibit similarities as shown in
Figure 3c where 𝐴and 𝐵are randomly placed in 𝑃𝐸0 and 𝑃𝐸2.
This strategy could also consider a random connection pattern as
shown in Figure 7a.
The second strategy is a greedy approach. This approach places
node 𝐴in the first available 𝑃𝐸, for example, 𝑃𝐸0. Then, it
places node 𝐵in the next available 𝑃𝐸, 𝑃𝐸1. Subsequently, the
algorithm checks the routing feasibility from 𝑃𝐸0 to 𝑃𝐸1. If the
routing is possible, it adds the routing path to the current map-
ping. However, if the routing is not possible, the greedy approach
assigns node 𝐵to the next available 𝑃𝐸, such as 𝑃𝐸2. If there
is no available and routable 𝑃𝐸𝑠to connect to node 𝐴(placed
in 𝑃𝐸0), the routing adds this edge to the set of unrouted edges
and evaluates the next edge. Ultimately, the greedy strategy pro-
duces a valid, complete routing or a partial routing with a set of
unrouted edges.
The third strategy is the Local Search (LS) approach. It begins by
executing the greedy placement strategy. If the greedy approach
fails to find a feasible routing for all edges, the Local Search
attempts to improve the routing by swapping the positions of two
nodes, denoted as 𝐴and 𝐵, if such a swap reduces the number of
unrouted edges. For example, let’s assume that the algorithm ini-
tially places node 𝐴in 𝑃𝐸0 and node 𝐵in 𝑃𝐸2. The LS evaluates
whether swapping the positions of 𝐴and 𝐵(placing 𝐵in 𝑃𝐸0 and
𝐴in 𝑃𝐸2) reduces the number of unrouted edges. For example,
Figure 7a shows a routing conflict between the connection pairs
7 →4 and 1 →6, that it solves by swapping 𝐴and 𝐵where there
is no conflict between 7 →4 and 6 →2. The algorithm termi-
nates when swapping nodes without increasing the number of
unrouted edges is impossible.
The last strategy is the meta-heuristic Simulated Annealing (SA).
SA prevents getting trapped in local minima within the solution
space by temporarily increasing the current routing cost. SA con-
ducts node swapping, even if it increases the number of unrouted
edges. SA starts from a random placement and performs the node
swaps to optimize the solution. Additionally, we execute LS as a
post-optimization step after the SA process.

routing follows a greedy approach. The next section introduces
novel routing strategies.

We propose to evaluate three strategies for assigning routing
codes to extra bits in a greedy manner. For example, consider a
connection pair 10101010 𝑋𝑋𝑋𝑋00111011 , where the first

all previously routed connections. If conflicts arise, the code is
iteratively incremented until a conflict-free code is found or rout-
ing fails for this connection pair.
The second strategy involves random assignment (RND), initi-
ating from a randomly selected code such as 𝑋𝑋𝑋𝑋= 1010.
If conflicts arise, the algorithm chooses a new random code
until finding a conflict-free assignment or evaluating all possi-
ble codes. The third strategy, the incremental approach (INC),
can be applied to both previous strategies. Instead of initiat-
ing with a code of 0 or a random code for a new connection
pair, it begins with the following available code. For instance,
assuming the pair 10101010 𝑋𝑋𝑋𝑋00111011 has been suc-
cessfully routed with 𝑋𝑋𝑋𝑋= 0000, the following code for the
subsequent pair will be 𝑋𝑋𝑋𝑋= 0001. If conflicts arise, the
algorithm inspects all subsequent codes in sequence, including
the code 𝑋𝑋𝑋𝑋= 0000 for the sequential strategy. In the case
of the random strategy, the algorithm first generates a random
permutation vector containing all codes. Then, it applies the
incremental approach to the sequence of codes in the vector.
4.4

Multicast Priority
The multi-stage network with at least log(𝑛) extra levels and/or
more complex and larger switches is rearrangeable for one-to-one
permutations using polynomial routing algorithms [14]. How-
ever, in multicast, the problem becomes NP-Complete [17]. A
fundamental principle for optimizing multicast connections is to
delay branching as much as possible [32]. We propose evaluating
a strategy that prioritizes multicast patterns. First, the placement
algorithm aims to select multicast outputs as close as possible to
the branch in the last stages. Second, the routing algorithm will
assign an extra bit code to the multicast connections and then
assign codes for the one-to-one connections.
4.5

Routing Code Heuristics
The preceding strategies all employ a greedy approach to assign-
ing extra codes. Once the algorithm executes a routing, it retains
its code even if it is impossible to route connections due to earlier
assignments. We evaluate Monte Carlo and simulated annealing
approaches to perform a space solution exploration.
The Monte Carlo tree search (MCTS) constructs a tree where
each node represents a decision point, assigning a code to a
pair of connections. The tree is incrementally built by simulating
random paths corresponding to different connection pair orders
until all connections are visited. For example, if we aim to route
2 →7, 3 →9, and 9 →1, and the initial connection is 2 →7, we
could generate two tree paths: 3 →9, 9 →1 and 9 →1, 3 →9.
MCTS generates 𝑚tree paths by exploring various connection
pair orders until reaching the final connections. Subsequently, we
select the best path with the highest success rate in establishing
connections. Following this, we construct a single path from the
root to connection pair 𝑡and conduct further exploration using 𝑘
different random order paths until reaching the last connection.
The concept is to identify the most promising solution from a set
of 𝑚random orders. Subsequently, we retain only the first 𝑡con-
nections for the best order while exploring 𝑘different random
orders for the remaining connections.
We also propose employing simulated annealing (SA) to swap
extra code bits. We assume that the input and output assignments
have already been determined during the placement step. In the
SA routing step, two random connection pairs will be selected,
and their extra code bit assignments will be swapped. Based on
the stochastic acceptance probability driven by the SA algorithm,
this swapping could be accepted if it reduces connection conflicts
or even if it increases conflicts.

This section summarizes our main results evaluating the place-

This study proposes evaluating placement and routing strategies

we define CW as the quotient of the number of need-to-be-routed
edges and the total size of available interconnections in the net-

In the case of all graphs, assuming there are no routing conflicts,

We executed all algorithms for each benchmark only once, except

algorithm and selected the best result out of the 10 runs. Con-

time-consuming strategy, with an average time of around 1.5 min,

improving the CGRA performance, enabling it to route graphs
with high workloads efficiently. Considering the vast solution
space of 10671 possibilities, SA’s exploration, utilizing the 𝑃𝐸
symmetry properties, yields interesting results.

Monte Carlo and Simulated Annealing
Simulated annealing is a successful strategy for placement, even
when routing uses a greedy approach. However, a few connec-
tions may not be routed due to greedy decisions. One approach is
to use simulated annealing to swap the routing code assignment
to mitigate code word string matching. Nevertheless, a simulated
annealing strategy based on swapping the routing code fails to
improve the routing rate. Therefore, we propose evaluating other
meta-heuristics.
We evaluate the Monte Carlo approach. The Monte Carlo
algorithm explores the solution tree by performing a deep dive,
pruning non-promising branches, then backtracking to the best
path and repeating the process by branching and exploring fur-
ther. Suppose we have a sequence of 10 connections. Assuming
the best sequence is 𝑎, 𝑏, 𝑐, 𝑑, 𝑒, 𝑓, 𝑔, ℎ, 𝑖, 𝑗, we keep the sequence
order up to the fourth element or 𝑎, 𝑏, 𝑐, 𝑑, and then generate
100 new sequence permutations for the remaining 6 connections.
Next, we select the best permutation, 𝑎, 𝑏, 𝑐, 𝑑, 𝑔, 𝑗, . . . . We keep
the first six connections and generate 100 new sequence permu-
tations for the remaining connections.
Table 9 compares the performance of the sequential approach
(the best initial approach) with the multicast priority (Mul) and
Monte Carlo (MCTS) approaches. First, even without additional
stages, the Mul and MCTS approaches achieve better results. This
behavior occurs because when the algorithm prioritizes multi-
cast connections, branches occur in the earlier stages, preserv-
ing more free paths. Second, the routing order can be significant
when not all connections can be routed. For example, if connec-
tion 𝐶1 conflicts with 𝐶2 and 𝐶3, routing 𝐶1 first prevents 𝐶2
and 𝐶3 from being routed. However, if 𝐶2 and 𝐶3 do not conflict
with each other, routing both 𝐶2 and 𝐶3 while excluding 𝐶1 can
increase the routing success rate.
The Monte Carlo approach improves the routing rate of the
Sequential approach by 3% to 7%. Given that we evaluate pat-
terns with a workload of 100%, this improvement translates to
routing 8 to 18 more connections. Assuming a maximum of
four additional stages, in scenarios with 20% and 40% multicast,
the Monte Carlo approach can route 235 and 244 connections,

The Omega or shuffle-exchange network [21] is a multi-stage
network with log 𝑁stages and 𝑛
2 switches. Initially designed to
connect a set of processors to a set of memories, this network
offers conflict-free access to common address patterns, such as
rows, columns, diagonals, and more [21]. Moreover, it has been
demonstrated that any one-to-one permutation pattern can be
routed using 𝑘extra stages [39] or by using log 𝑛stages of an
Omega network concatenated with log 𝑛stages of an Omega−1
network [12], resulting in a rearrangeable network. However,
for more complex patterns, including multicast [13], if the
single-pass routing fails, they need to be divided into a minimum
number of groups (passes) to establish conflict-free paths for all
pairs in each group simultaneously [40]. Therefore, this approach
slows down the parallel communication by serializing the
groups. The challenge is the huge solution space to reach a valid
configuration when the network size exceeds 16 connections.
Recent work on high-performance FPGAs [5, 6] has demon-
strated that even for 32 connections, a log 𝑛butterfly multi-stage
network in packet-switching mode improves bandwidth by
4× to 200 GB/s. Nevertheless, the theoretical peak bandwidth
is 430 GB/s [5], and thus the packet-switching multi-stage
achieves less than 50% of the maximum potential throughput.
This approach has been employed to create reconfigurable HBM
FPGA accelerators for large graph traversal problems, including
single-source shortest path (SSSP) [6], PageRank, breadth-first
search, closeness centrality [8], sparse matrix vector [7], and
sorting algorithms [5, 41]. While packet-switching mode demon-
strates a bandwidth upper bound of 50% for 50% of the workload
without extra levels, replacing the butterfly topology with a
shuffle-exchange network that can include additional levels
allows a better exploration of the search space for developing
novel dynamic routing to get close to 100% bandwidth. First,
shuffle-exchange networks have the same inter-stage pattern and
have shown superior performance compared to other multi-stage
networks [2]. Second, our results in Section 5.1.1 indicate that
reaching 100% bandwidth is possible even in random patterns by
using 2–4 extra levels in a 256-interconnection network.
Furthermore, using circuit-switching in more static streaming
scenarios could reduce the resource usage of flip-flops and
Look-Up Tables (LUTs) in multi-stage FPGA design [5, 9]. A
butterfly network has the connection pattern of a “half” Benes
network, suggesting a Benes network could be viewed as a
butterfly with the maximum number of extra stages. However,
even the Benes network remains blocked in the presence of mul-
ticast. We propose to use a shuffle-exchange network that could
potentially be rearrangeable with log 𝑛extra stages, which is an
open problem. We demonstrate that in an 8 × 8 network space,
shuffle-exchange can be rearrangeable using GPU exploration
despite the exponentially large search space, even for small
networks. A recent work [42] proposes using a copy and a Benes
network to handle multicast, but this approach doubles the
number of stages using 4 log 𝑛stages, rendering it impractical for
larger networks, in comparison to our approach that uses 2 log 𝑛
stages in the worst case. As a proof-of-concept, the copy-Benes
approach [42] limited its FPGA prototype to 32 connections when
solving linear equations. A more promising alternative, similar to
our proposal, was recently presented in reference [43] for convo-
lution network accelerators in FPGAs, utilizing two back-to-back
butterfly networks to handle multicast patterns, however, it was
not evaluated for large size (greater than 16). Recently, a variant

Conclusion
Efficient parallel communication stands as one of the significant
challenges. Multi-stage networks mitigate the cost and offer
a network with 𝑂(𝑛log(𝑛)) switches, but they introduce chal-
lenges in routing. They may lead to blocking, thereby requiring
serialization of communication. In the case of large multi-stage
networks with 256 connections, the configuration space explodes
to 10671 possibilities in the presence of multicast, which is one
of the major challenges of this work. Despite that, we have
demonstrated that a greedy placement approach, enhanced by
Local Search or stochastic Simulated Annealing techniques,
can efficiently perform routing without extra stages. For 256
connections, our approach enables the routing of graphs with up
to 200 operators, effectively doubling the performance compared
to previous multi-stage CGRA frameworks [9]. Our placement
approach utilizes the high symmetry properties inherent in the
CGRA architecture. In addition, we propose routing strategies
tailored for high workload scenarios. We demonstrate that
the Benes network is blocking in the presence of multicast,
suggesting that variable-length extra-level networks, such as
shuffle-exchange, should be explored. New routing strategies
based on sequential or incremental coding, coupled with prior-
itizing multicast connections and utilizing the Monte Carlo tree
search approach, can significantly improve routing capability
despite performing only a limited exploration of the vast solution
search space. Therefore, the main insight of this work is that
routing large multi-stage networks is challenging. However,
it is possible to achieve 90% workload using Monte Carlo and
multicast methods, and even 100% when placement is optimized
using simulated annealing and local search. Additionally, to the
best of the authors’ knowledge, we prove that the Benes network
is not rearrangeable in the presence of multicast patterns using
exhaustive search and GPU simulations.

Abstract: High-performance computing demands efficient and scalable interconnections. Although crossbar networks offer high parallel bandwidth, their 𝑂(𝑛2) costs are prohibitively expensive. Multi-stage networks provide scalability with 𝑂(𝑛log 𝑛) cost, yet they may block certain routing patterns. Rearrangeable multistage networks (RMNs) have emerged as a cost-effective solution, enabling internal connection rearrangements to make all paths accessible without network blocking. However, discovering optimal rear- rangement strategies remains a challenge for unblocking large-scale (256 connections) reconfigurable networks. We advance the state of the art by effectively managing workloads with over 50% without blocking. When nearly all connections are required, we introduce routing strategies to rearrange existing connections. In the presence of multicast, where the configuration space exceeds 10671, we propose novel strategies employing simulated annealing for placement and Monte Carlo tree search for routing to pri- oritize multicast connections, which simultaneously maximize the number of connections by minimizing conflicts and reducing the number of extra stages. To the best of our knowledge, we first demonstrate that the Benes network is not rearrangeable under multicast conditions. We propose exploring the rearrangeability of shuffle exchanges with additional network stages.
